# Understanding the MICS6 reading assessment {#c02-reading}

Reading is the most complex part of the MICS6 Foundational Learning Skills data.

At first glance the assessment appears straightforward: a child reads a story and answers comprehension questions. In the microdata, however, several earlier decisions determine **whether the child reaches the story, which story they receive, and how their subsequent data should be interpreted**.

Understanding this sequence is essential before constructing reading outcomes.

## Overview of the reading assessment

At a high level, the assessment involves:

```text
Eligible child age 7–14
          │
          ▼
Permission / child participation
          │
          ▼
Determine assessment language
          │
          ▼
Does the child agree to read?
          │
          ▼
Practice / routing where applicable
          │
          ▼
Read story
          │
          ├── words attempted
          ├── words missed / read incorrectly
          │
          ▼
Comprehension questions
          │
          ├── 3 literal
          └── 2 inferential
```

The exact country questionnaire should always be consulted because language options and country adaptations differ.

## Assessment language is part of the data-generating process

The standard MICS6 questionnaire asks about the language the child speaks at home and, for children with schooling experience, the language used by teachers.

The questionnaire then uses this information to determine whether an appropriate reading booklet is available and which language should be used for the reading task.

In the standard questionnaire:

- `FL7` records the language spoken most of the time at home;
- `FL9A/FL9B` asks about the language used by teachers for children with schooling experience; and
- the subsequent reading instructions route the child to an available reading booklet/language.

This means that reading performance cannot always be separated from **assessment-language availability and assignment**.

In multilingual surveys, countries may have more than one reading passage. As discussed in [Getting data from IPUMS MICS](#c01-ipums), this is also why the IPUMS reading variables are unsafe to use for multi-passage countries.

## Not every eligible child attempts the story

There are several reasons an age-eligible child may have no story-reading result.

For example:

```text
age 7–14
   │
   ├── permission not given
   ├── child does not participate
   ├── suitable assessment language unavailable
   ├── child declines reading
   ├── routed out through practice sequence
   └── attempts main story
```

These pathways do not all have the same substantive meaning.

A child who was never offered an appropriate passage because of language availability is different from a child who attempted a passage but could not read it. Treating both simply as `NA` obscures that distinction.

This is why AFLEARN constructs a research-ready **reading-status variable**. The variable records whether the child reached the reading task and, where they did not, the reason for the missing reading result.

The construction is provided in [Constructing MICS6 reading outcomes](#c03-reading).

## Practice items and routing

The standard MICS6 reading sequence contains practice/routing items before the main story for some children.

The routing depends partly on age and schooling experience. Researchers should therefore **not infer inability to read simply because the main story variables are missing**.

The correct interpretation requires following the questionnaire skip pattern.

AFLEARN's processing script does this explicitly rather than relying on missingness in the final story variables.

## Oral reading accuracy

For children who attempt the main story, the interviewer records reading performance.

The official foundational-reading definition requires the child to read **at least 90% of the story words correctly**.

Conceptually:

```text
words read correctly
--------------------  >= 0.90
 total story words
```

The difficulty is that the denominator — **total story words** — is not provided as a simple analysis variable in all released country datasets.

Moreover, story length can vary with country and language adaptation.

::: {.alternativebox-header}
**You cannot calculate the 90% accuracy criterion correctly without the passage length**
:::

::: {.alternativebox}
Counting only the child's attempted or incorrect words is insufficient unless you also know how many words were in the passage the child received.
:::

AFLEARN therefore created a **passage-length variable** from the country assessment materials and an **assessment-language variable** identifying the relevant passage.

These are used in the research-ready reading construction in Section 3.

## Literal comprehension

Children who progress through the reading task are asked **three literal comprehension questions**.

Literal questions ask about information stated directly in the story.

Under the MICS foundational-reading definition, the child must answer **all three** correctly to satisfy the literal-comprehension component.

## Inferential comprehension

Children are also asked **two inferential comprehension questions**.

These require the child to draw meaning from information that is implied rather than simply repeat a stated fact.

The child must answer **both** correctly to satisfy the inferential-comprehension component.

## The overall foundational reading indicator

The official MICS definition combines all three components:

```text
READING ACCURACY
>= 90% of story words correct
           │
           AND
           │
3/3 LITERAL QUESTIONS CORRECT
           │
           AND
           │
2/2 INFERENTIAL QUESTIONS CORRECT
           │
           ▼
FOUNDATIONAL READING SKILLS
```

UNICEF's MICS6 statistical analysis manual describes this as a conjunctive indicator: the child must satisfy the accuracy, literal-comprehension and inferential-comprehension requirements.

## Why the raw reading variables are not enough for our purposes

For multi-country analysis, researchers face three related problems.

### 1. Passage length

The released datasets do not provide a single harmonised variable giving the number of words in the passage administered to each child.

### 2. Assessment language and passage

Countries with more than one reading language can have multiple sets of passage variables. Researchers need to identify which passage the child actually attempted.

### 3. Complex skip patterns

A blank story result can arise for different reasons. Without reconstructing the questionnaire pathway, it is easy to classify children incorrectly or silently change the analysis sample.

AFLEARN's research-ready variables address all three problems.

## What AFLEARN adds

The Section 3 processing produces variables that make the reading data easier to analyse transparently, including:

- **assessment language**;
- **passage length**;
- **reading status**;
- reading accuracy measures;
- literal-comprehension measures;
- inferential-comprehension measures; and
- an overall foundational-reading indicator.

The detailed harmonisation and country-specific derivations will be documented separately in the technical appendix. Most users of this guide do not need to reproduce that work; they need to understand what the derived variables mean and how to use them correctly.

## A note on cross-country comparisons

Reading comparisons deserve more caution than numeracy comparisons because reading is inherently language dependent.

Differences across countries may reflect not only underlying reading skill but also features such as:

- language of instruction;
- language spoken at home;
- language in which the child was assessed;
- linguistic characteristics of the assessment language;
- country adaptation of the story; and
- the relationship between the assessment language and the child's schooling experience.

The MICS6 assessment was designed for national monitoring and uses country/language adaptation. Researchers should therefore avoid interpreting a difference in raw reading performance across countries as if every child completed an identical language-neutral test.

These issues do not make cross-country analysis impossible, but they should shape the research question and interpretation.
